questions.question: What is the primary approach called when we conserve and protect the whole ecosystem to save biodiversity at all levels?
questions.explanation: In situ conservation refers to protecting the entire ecosystem in its natural habitat, which automatically saves all levels of biodiversity. This is the on-site approach where we save the entire forest to save the tiger.

questions.question: How many biodiversity hotspots were initially identified by conservationists?
questions.explanation: Initially, 25 biodiversity hotspots were identified by conservationists. Subsequently, nine more were added, bringing the total to 34 biodiversity hotspots worldwide.

questions.question: What is the current total number of biodiversity hotspots in the world?
questions.explanation: The current total number of biodiversity hotspots is 34, after initially identifying 25 and subsequently adding 9 more to the list.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three biodiversity hotspots that cover India's exceptionally high biodiversity regions?
questions.explanation: The three biodiversity hotspots covering India's rich biodiversity regions are Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya. The Deccan Plateau is not listed as a biodiversity hotspot.

questions.question: What percentage of the earth's land area do all biodiversity hotspots collectively cover?
questions.explanation: All biodiversity hotspots put together cover less than 2% of the earth's land area, yet they harbour an extremely high number of species.

questions.question: What percentage of ongoing mass extinctions could be reduced by strict protection of biodiversity hotspots?
questions.explanation: Strict protection of biodiversity hotspots could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30%, according to the text.

questions.question: How many biosphere reserves does India currently have?
questions.explanation: India currently has 14 biosphere reserves that protect ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions.

questions.question: How many national parks are there in India?
questions.explanation: India has 90 national parks that serve as legally protected areas for biodiversity conservation.

questions.question: How many wildlife sanctuaries does India have?
questions.explanation: India has 448 wildlife sanctuaries that provide protection to various animal species and their habitats.

questions.question: What are sacred groves in the context of Indian biodiversity conservation?
options: Tracts of forest set aside for religious protection where trees and wildlife are venerated and given total protection
Urban parks designed for recreational activities
questions.explanation: Sacred groves are tracts of forest set aside in many Indian cultures where all trees and wildlife within are venerated and given total protection based on religious and cultural traditions.

questions.question: In which state are the sacred groves the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened species?
questions.explanation: In Meghalaya, the sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plant and animal species.

questions.question: Which of the following regions does NOT have sacred groves mentioned in the text?

Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra
questions.explanation: The text mentions sacred groves in Khasi and Jaintia Hills (Meghalaya), Aravalli Hills (Rajasthan), Western Ghat regions (Karnataka and Maharashtra), and Sarguja, Chanda, Bastar areas (Madhya Pradesh). Eastern Ghats of Tamil Nadu is not mentioned.

questions.question: What is ex situ conservation?
options: Protecting species in their natural habitat
Taking threatened animals and plants out from their natural habitat and placing them in special settings for protection
Allowing species to evolve naturally without human intervention
Creating artificial ecosystems in urban areas
questions.explanation: Ex situ conservation is the off-site approach where threatened animals and plants are taken from their natural habitat and placed in special settings like zoological parks, botanical gardens, and wildlife safari parks for protection and special care.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method of ex situ conservation mentioned in the text?
questions.explanation: Wildlife sanctuaries are part of in situ conservation, not ex situ. The text mentions zoological parks, botanical gardens, and wildlife safari parks as ex situ conservation methods.

questions.question: What modern technique allows preservation of gametes of threatened species in viable and fertile condition for long periods?
questions.explanation: Cryopreservation is the technique that allows gametes of threatened species to be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods.

questions.question: What technique allows eggs to be fertilised outside the body in ex situ conservation?
questions.explanation: In vitro fertilisation is the technique mentioned in the text that allows eggs to be fertilised outside the body as part of advanced ex situ conservation methods.

questions.question: Which method can be used to propagate plants in ex situ conservation?
questions.explanation: Tissue culture methods are mentioned in the text as a way to propagate plants in ex situ conservation settings.

questions.question: Where can seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants be kept for long periods?
questions.explanation: Seed banks are mentioned in the text as places where seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods.

questions.question: In which year and city was the historic Convention on Biological Diversity (The Earth Summit) held?
questions.explanation: The historic Convention on Biological Diversity, also known as The Earth Summit, was held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.

questions.question: In which year and city was the World Summit on Sustainable Development held?
questions.explanation: The World Summit on Sustainable Development was held in 2002 in Johannesburg, South Africa, where 190 countries pledged commitment to reduce biodiversity loss.

questions.question: How many countries pledged their commitment at the World Summit on Sustainable Development?
questions.explanation: 190 countries pledged their commitment at the World Summit on Sustainable Development held in Johannesburg in 2002.

questions.question: What does the term 'biodiversity hotspot' primarily refer to?
options: Areas with the highest human population density
Regions with very high levels of species richness and high degree of endemism
Urban areas with maximum green cover
Agricultural regions with maximum crop diversity
questions.explanation: Biodiversity hotspots are regions with very high levels of species richness and high degree of endemism (species confined to that region and not found anywhere else).

questions.question: What is the meaning of 'endemism' in the context of biodiversity hotspots?
options: Species that can survive in any environment
Species confined to a particular region and not found anywhere else
questions.explanation: Endemism refers to species that are confined to a particular region and are not found anywhere else in the world.

questions.question: Why are biodiversity hotspots also described as regions of accelerated habitat loss?
options: Because they have the highest rainfall
Because they are experiencing rapid destruction of natural habitats due to human activities
Because they are located near volcanic areas
Because they have the oldest geological formations
questions.explanation: Biodiversity hotspots are also regions of accelerated habitat loss because they are experiencing rapid destruction of natural habitats due to various human activities, making conservation efforts urgent.

questions.question: Which approach to conservation is described as 'on site' conservation?
questions.explanation: In situ conservation is described as 'on site' conservation because it involves protecting species in their natural habitat.

questions.question: Which approach to conservation is described as 'off site' conservation?
questions.explanation: Ex situ conservation is described as 'off site' conservation because it involves taking threatened species out of their natural habitat and placing them in special settings for protection.

questions.question: What is the main conflict that nations face regarding biodiversity conservation?
questions.explanation: The text states that many nations face the conflict between development and conservation, making it unrealistic and economically not feasible to conserve all their biological wealth.

questions.question: What happens to animals that have become extinct in the wild but are maintained in zoological parks?

They continue to be maintained in zoological parks as part of ex situ conservation
They are used for commercial trading
They are converted to domestic animals
questions.explanation: The text mentions that many animals have become extinct in the wild but continue to be maintained in zoological parks as part of ex situ conservation efforts.

questions.question: What does the text say about biodiversity and political boundaries?

Biodiversity is highest in politically stable regions
Biodiversity is managed by political parties
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that biodiversity knows no political boundaries and its conservation is a collective responsibility of all nations.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Convention on Biological Diversity?
options: To promote commercial use of biological resources
To call upon all nations to take appropriate measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable utilisation of its benefits
To create new species through genetic engineering
questions.explanation: The Convention on Biological Diversity called upon all nations to take appropriate measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable utilisation of its benefits.

They conduct DNA sequencing of all known organisms

Less year-to-year variation in total biomass
No change in biomass variation over time

questions.question: What does the 'rivet popper hypothesis' proposed by Paul Ehrlich compare species to?
questions.explanation: Paul Ehrlich's rivet popper hypothesis compares species to rivets in an airplane. Just as removing rivets one by one weakens the plane, species extinction weakens ecosystem functioning. The rivets on the wings represent key species that drive major ecosystem functions.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of biodiversity loss in a region?

Increased variability in ecosystem processes like water use
Enhanced stability and productivity of the ecosystem

questions.question: How much faster are current species extinction rates compared to pre-human times?

questions.question: How many more hectares of rain forest would have been lost by the time you finish reading the chapter?
questions.explanation: The text states that by the time you finish reading this chapter, 1000 more hectares of rain forest would have been lost.

questions.question: The Amazon rain forest is being cut and cleared for which of the following purposes?
options: For cultivating soya beans or conversion to grasslands for raising beef cattle
questions.explanation: The text states that the Amazon rain forest is being cut and cleared for cultivating soya beans or for conversion to grasslands for raising beef cattle.

questions.question: Which animals are badly affected when large habitats are broken up into small fragments?
options: Mammals and birds requiring large territories and certain migratory animals
questions.explanation: The text states that when large habitats are broken up into small fragments, mammals and birds requiring large territories and certain animals with migratory habits are badly affected.

questions.question: According to the text, over-exploitation occurs when what happens?
options: When humans stop using natural resources
questions.explanation: The text states that humans have always depended on nature for food and shelter, but when 'need' turns to 'greed', it leads to over-exploitation of natural resources.

questions.question: How are alien species introduced according to the text?
options: Unintentionally or deliberately for whatever purpose
questions.explanation: The text states that alien species are introduced unintentionally or deliberately for whatever purpose, and some of them turn invasive.

questions.question: What is the current situation of many marine fish populations around the world?
options: They are protected by international laws
questions.explanation: The text states that presently many marine fish populations around the world are over harvested, endangering the continued existence of some commercially important species.

questions.question: Besides total habitat loss, what else threatens the survival of many species?
options: The degradation of many habitats by pollution
questions.explanation: The text states that besides total loss, the degradation of many habitats by pollution also threatens the survival of many species.

questions.question: What is co-extinction according to the text?
options: When two species compete for the same resource
When a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct
questions.explanation: The text defines co-extinction as when a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct.

questions.question: What are the three categories of arguments for conserving biodiversity mentioned in the textbook?
options: Narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian, and ethical arguments
questions.explanation: The textbook explicitly states that reasons for conserving biodiversity can be grouped into three categories: narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian, and ethical arguments.

questions.question: According to the textbook, what percentage of drugs currently sold worldwide are derived from plants?
questions.explanation: The textbook states that more than 25 per cent of the drugs currently sold in the market worldwide are derived from plants.

questions.question: How many species of plants contribute to traditional medicines used by native peoples around the world?
questions.explanation: The textbook mentions that 25,000 species of plants contribute to the traditional medicines used by native peoples around the world.

questions.question: What is bioprospecting as defined in the textbook?
options: Searching for new species in deep oceans
Exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance
Collecting seeds from all forests for storage
questions.explanation: The textbook defines bioprospecting as exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance.

questions.question: What percentage of total oxygen in Earth's atmosphere is estimated to be produced by the Amazon forest through photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: The textbook states that the fast-dwindling Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a pollinator in the ecosystem services discussion?
questions.explanation: The textbook mentions bees, bumblebees, birds and bats as pollinators. Butterflies are not mentioned in this context.

questions.question: What does the ethical argument for conserving biodiversity emphasize?
options: Economic profits from selling forest products
Every species has intrinsic value regardless of economic value
Creating more jobs in the tourism sector
questions.explanation: The ethical argument states that every species has an intrinsic value, even if it may not be of current or any economic value to us, and we have a moral duty to care for their well-being.

questions.question: What is the meaning of in situ conservation?
options: Conservation in zoos and botanical gardens
On site conservation where the whole ecosystem is protected
questions.explanation: The textbook defines in situ conservation as protecting the whole ecosystem so that biodiversity at all levels is protected in its natural habitat.

questions.question: When is ex situ conservation considered the desirable approach?
options: When species are abundant in the wild
When an organism is endangered and needs urgent measures to save it from extinction
When there is no human interference
questions.explanation: The textbook states that ex situ conservation is desirable when an animal or plant is endangered or threatened and needs urgent measures to save it from extinction in the wild.

questions.question: How many biodiversity hotspots were initially identified, and what is the total number now?
questions.explanation: The textbook states that initially 25 biodiversity hotspots were identified, but subsequently nine more were added, bringing the total to 34.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three biodiversity hotspots that cover India's rich biodiversity regions?
questions.explanation: The textbook mentions three hotspots covering India: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya. Sundaland is not mentioned as covering India.

questions.question: How many wildlife sanctuaries does India currently have according to the textbook?
questions.explanation: The textbook states that India now has 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks and 448 wildlife sanctuaries.

questions.question: What percentage of the world's land area does India have, and what percentage of global species diversity does it contribute?
questions.explanation: India has only 2.4% of the world's land area but contributes an impressive 8.1% of global species diversity, making it one of the 12 mega diversity countries.

questions.question: How many species of plants have been recorded from India according to the text?
questions.explanation: Nearly 45,000 species of plants have been recorded from India, and twice as many animal species have also been documented.

questions.question: According to Robert May's estimates, what percentage of total species have been recorded so far globally?
questions.explanation: If we accept May's global estimates, only 22% of the total species have been recorded so far, meaning 78% remain undiscovered.

questions.question: What is the latitudinal range that defines the tropics according to the text?
options: 0 degrees to 30 degrees N and S
questions.explanation: The tropics are defined as the latitudinal range of 23.5 degrees N to 23.5 degrees S, which harbour more species than temperate or polar areas.

questions.question: How many bird species does Colombia have compared to New York and Greenland?
questions.explanation: Colombia located near the equator has nearly 1,400 species of birds, while New York at 41 degrees N has 105 species and Greenland at 71 degrees N only 56 species, demonstrating the latitudinal gradient.

questions.question: The Amazonian rainforest is home to approximately how many species of invertebrates?
questions.explanation: The Amazonian rainforest is home to more than 1,25,000 invertebrates, along with 40,000+ plants, 3,000 fishes, 1,300 birds, 427 mammals, 427 amphibians, and 378 reptiles.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the hypotheses proposed to explain greater biological diversity in the tropics?
options: Tropical regions have had more evolutionary time due to less disturbance
Tropical environments are less seasonal and more constant
Tropical regions receive more solar energy contributing to higher productivity
Tropical regions have larger land area than temperate regions
questions.explanation: The three hypotheses are: (a) tropics had long evolutionary time due to less disturbance, (b) less seasonal and more constant environments promote niche specialisation, and (c) more solar energy available contributes to higher productivity. Larger land area is not mentioned as a hypothesis.

questions.question: What percentage of all recorded species are animals according to the text?
questions.explanation: The text explicitly states that more than 70 percent of all the species recorded are animals.

questions.question: What percentage of total species do plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) comprise?
questions.explanation: The text states that plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) comprise no more than 22 percent of the total.

questions.question: Which taxonomic group makes up more than 70% of the total animals?
questions.explanation: Among animals, insects are the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up more than 70 percent of the total animals.

questions.question: According to the text, out of every 10 animals on this planet, how many are insects?
questions.explanation: The text states that out of every 10 animals on this planet, 7 are insects.

questions.question: The number of fungi species in the world is more than the combined total of which groups?
questions.explanation: The number of fungi species in the world is more than the combined total of the species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.

questions.question: What does Figure 13.1 depict?
options: Proportionate number of species of major taxa of plants, invertebrates and vertebrates
questions.explanation: Figure 13.1 represents global biodiversity showing the proportionate number of species of major taxa of plants, invertebrates and vertebrates.

questions.question: Why are prokaryotes not included in the species estimates mentioned?
options: They are not considered living organisms
Biologists are not sure about how many prokaryotic species there might be
They are too small to count
questions.explanation: Biologists are not sure about how many prokaryotic species there might be, and conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species.

questions.question: What is the problem with identifying prokaryotic species using conventional methods?
options: They are too large to study
Conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species
questions.explanation: The problem is that conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species and many species are simply not culturable under laboratory conditions.

questions.question: If biochemical or molecular criteria are used for delineating prokaryotic species, what might happen to their diversity estimate?
options: Their diversity alone might run into millions
questions.explanation: If we accept biochemical or molecular criteria for delineating species for this group, then their diversity alone might run into millions.

questions.question: Which of the following is shown in the Invertebrates pie chart in Figure 13.1?
options: Insects, Molluscs, Crustaceans, Other animal groups
questions.explanation: The Invertebrates pie chart shows Insects, Molluscs, Crustaceans, and Other animal groups.

questions.question: Which of the following is shown in the Vertebrates pie chart in Figure 13.1?
questions.explanation: The Vertebrates pie chart shows Fishes, Amphibians, Reptiles, Birds, and Mammals.

questions.question: Which of the following is shown in the Plants pie chart in Figure 13.1?
options: Angiosperms, Fungi, Algae, Lichens, Mosses, Ferns and allies
questions.explanation: The Plants pie chart shows Angiosperms, Fungi, Algae, Lichens, Mosses, and Ferns and allies.

questions.question: Why are many microbial species not identifiable under laboratory conditions?
options: They are too large to observe
They are not culturable under laboratory conditions
They do not exist in nature
questions.explanation: Many species are simply not culturable under laboratory conditions, making them difficult to identify using conventional methods.

questions.question: What is the most species-rich taxonomic group among animals?
questions.explanation: Among animals, insects are the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up more than 70 percent of the total.

questions.question: The text mentions that plants include which of the following groups?
options: Algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms
questions.explanation: The text states that plants include algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms.
